payload.throughline: Locate the new element, classify its directional impact, revise only what it warrants, and compare additions by the change they force.

learner_content_blocks: Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: State a passage claim and one relation that supports it, then distinguish that map from any outside knowledge you happen to have.

Starting observation: A passage says a library added evening workshops to reach adults whose jobs prevent daytime attendance. New information says most evening participants work daytime shifts. Which passage component should be compared with the new information first?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: connect a supplied new element to the exact part of the passage model it bears on. The first move is placement, not impact. This lesson assumes the two packet-declared prerequisite lessons. If either prerequisite check is insecure, stop rather than guessing: hand off to V3-LES-191933 via V3-EDG-585563 or to V3-LES-556584 via V3-EDG-768381.
Build a compact passage model: central claim, reasons, conditions, and named mechanisms. Then restate the new element in neutral terms.
Ask which model component would have to be true, false, narrower, or broader for the new element to matter. Stop after naming that relation; support or contradiction is a later judgment.
Use a two-column bridge: NEW ELEMENT on the left, TOUCHED PASSAGE COMPONENT on the right. Draw one justified link before assigning any direction.

I ignore whether I agree with the new statement. I scan the passage model for repeated nouns and, more importantly, the relation the statement changes. I choose the narrowest touched component and reject merely topical matches.
A passage argues that evening museum hours expand access because daytime work prevents attendance. A new survey says many evening visitors work standard daytime shifts.
The survey first bears on the passage relation between work schedules and evening attendance. It does not yet settle whether the access argument is strengthened or weakened.
Guided placement: name the passage component touched by the supplied fact. Use the prompt’s relation words before considering impact.
Less support: identify the narrowest touched claim or mechanism from a fresh passage model.
On your own: connect the new element to one exact model component without using outside facts.
Boundary: shared topic is not enough. A fact about trees does not bear on a tree-policy argument unless it touches the argument’s claim, mechanism, condition, or evidence.
Near exit: locate where a new observation bears on a familiar claim-and-mechanism model.
Changed exit: read a condition map rather than ordinary prose and identify the exact relation altered by a new constraint.
Repair the placement function: copy one phrase from the new element, locate the passage relation using that phrase, and state “This bears on ___ because ___.” Do not classify impact.
Fresh re-entry: place a new observation against a new passage model using the same narrow relation-finding function.
Repair the changed representation: translate each box in the condition map into a sentence, then link the new condition to the one box whose relation it changes.
Fresh changed re-entry: locate the touched condition in an unexposed map with new entities and relations.
Recap: model the passage, restate the new element neutrally, and link it to the narrowest passage component before judging direction.

Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: First locate the supplied element against one exact passage component; if that placement cannot be made, use the declared prerequisite handoff rather than classifying by topic.

Starting observation: A passage says all community theaters rely entirely on ticket sales. New information says one theater receives half its budget from a city grant. What is the most precise effect on the quoted claim?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: classify what a supplied element does to the exact passage relation already located. Direction follows placement. This lesson assumes the two packet-declared prerequisite lessons. If either prerequisite check is insecure, stop rather than guessing: hand off to V3-LES-191933 via V3-EDG-585563 or to V3-LES-556584 via V3-EDG-768381.
Support makes the relation more credible; contradiction points the other way; coexistence leaves it largely untouched because both can be true.
Qualification narrows a relation’s range or conditions. Negation removes a necessary or universal relation entirely. Use the passage’s quantifiers and conditions rather than outside truth.
Picture a dial attached to one passage claim: up is support, down is contradiction, sideways is coexistence, narrower is qualification, and off is negation.
I quote the smallest relevant passage claim, preserve its quantifier, and compare the new element. I reject an answer that classifies the topic rather than the logical relation.
A passage claims that every neighborhood market closes before dusk. New information identifies two markets that remain open until midnight.
The examples defeat “every,” so they negate the universal version. If the passage had said “most,” the same information might only qualify it.
Guided direction check: identify the passage quantifier and choose the directional relation it licenses.
Less support: classify a new condition after locating the exact claim it touches.
On your own: distinguish contradiction from qualification and coexistence.
Boundary: a fact can share the passage topic yet coexist without changing the claim. Relevance is not automatically support or contradiction.
Near exit: classify a fresh element against an explicit passage claim.
Changed exit: use a claim-condition table and determine whether a new case narrows, reverses, or leaves the model intact.

Repair the direction function: rewrite the passage claim as “if/then” or with its quantifier, then insert the new element and observe whether the relation rises, falls, narrows, disappears, or stays separate.
Fresh re-entry: classify a new element against a new explicit claim without reusing the exposed scenario.
Repair the scope function: mark words such as all, only, usually, and under these conditions. Decide whether the new case changes that scope before choosing a direction.
Fresh changed re-entry: classify an unexposed case from a new condition table.
Recap: locate first, preserve scope, then classify support, contradiction, coexistence, qualification, or negation.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Locate the new element and classify its directional impact before revising; if either operation is unavailable, use the exact declared prerequisite handoff.
Starting observation: A passage claims a reading room is quiet throughout every weekday. New information says construction makes it noisy on Fridays. Which revision is best bounded?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: revise only the model component the new information warrants and preserve the rest. Revision is not replacement. This lesson assumes the two packet-declared prerequisite lessons. If either prerequisite check is insecure, stop rather than guessing: hand off to V3-LES-191933 via V3-EDG-585563 or to V3-LES-556584 via V3-EDG-768381.
Start with the baseline claim. Mark the exact relation affected and its directional impact. Edit the fewest words or links needed to accommodate that impact.
Run a preservation check: every reason, condition, and relation untouched by the new element should remain. Do not import a new outside thesis.
Treat the passage model as a map under version control: change one justified line, keep every unaffected line, and record why the edit was necessary.

I compare candidate revisions against the original. I reject one that overreacts, introduces outside claims, or deletes unaffected support. The best revision is bounded but fully accommodates the new element.
A passage says weekly street markets increase foot traffic in all seasons. New counts show the increase in spring through autumn but no winter change.
A bounded revision is: weekly markets increase foot traffic in warmer seasons. The market-to-traffic relation remains; only its seasonal scope changes.
Guided revision: identify the affected phrase, revise it, and name one unaffected relation that must remain.
Less support: choose the smallest revision that fully accommodates a new case.
On your own: revise a thesis without replacing its topic, reasons, or unaffected conditions.
Boundary: “the passage is entirely wrong” is not a bounded revision when one condition changes. A revision must be proportional to the supplied element.
Near exit: select a minimal revision to a familiar claim while preserving unaffected support.
Changed exit: edit a multi-link argument map after a new element changes one link but leaves two others intact.
Repair the minimal-edit function: underline the smallest contradicted or qualified phrase, replace only that phrase, and read the revised sentence against the new element.
Fresh re-entry: revise a new claim with a different topic and unexposed wording.
Repair the preservation function: list each link in the baseline map, mark only the touched link, and rebuild the map with every unmarked link unchanged.
Fresh changed re-entry: revise one link in a new argument map and preserve the remaining links.
Recap: revise the touched relation enough to fit the new element, then verify that every unaffected relation survives.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Represent the central thesis and supporting relations before comparing candidate additions; use the exact prerequisite handoff if that model cannot be stated.

Starting observation: A passage argues that neighborhood newsletters strengthen civic participation by reporting local decisions in accessible language. Which addition would alter that argument least?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: choose the supplied addition that is compatible with the passage and consumes the smallest change budget. Truth outside the passage and shared wording do not decide. This lesson assumes the two packet-declared prerequisite lessons. If either prerequisite check is insecure, stop rather than guessing: hand off to V3-LES-191933 via V3-EDG-585563 or to V3-LES-556584 via V3-EDG-768381.
For each candidate, test compatibility with the central thesis, then count which central and supporting relations would need revision.
Reject an addition that contradicts a necessary relation. Among compatible candidates, prefer the one that preserves the thesis and the greatest number of supporting links.
Give each candidate a change budget: zero for preserved links, one for a narrowed support, and a large cost for replacing the thesis. Choose the compatible candidate with the lowest central cost.
I do not choose the option that sounds most like the passage. I insert each candidate into the model, trace the revisions it forces, and compare centrality before counting surface overlap.
A passage argues that small local festivals build civic connection through repeated face-to-face encounters. One addition says some festivals also stream performances for home viewers.

The streaming fact can coexist as an added access channel while leaving the face-to-face mechanism intact. An addition claiming remote viewing always replaces local gathering would demand a larger thesis change.
Guided comparison: eliminate incompatible additions, then compare how many central relations each remaining addition changes.
Less support: choose by model preservation, not by repeated vocabulary.
On your own: identify the compatible addition with the smallest central revision.
Boundary: an addition can repeat the passage’s nouns yet reverse its argument. Surface similarity does not establish compatibility or minimal change.
Near exit: compare additions against a familiar thesis-and-support model.
Changed exit: use a relation matrix to choose the addition with the smallest central change across several links.
Repair compatibility: test each candidate against the thesis first. Cross out any candidate that cannot coexist without replacing that thesis.
Fresh re-entry: compare new additions against a new passage model.
Repair the change budget: mark each relation a candidate preserves, narrows, or replaces; weight the central thesis more than a peripheral detail.
Fresh changed re-entry: apply the change budget to an unexposed relation matrix.
Recap: require compatibility, trace revisions, weight central relations, and choose the addition that changes the passage model least.
